suggested_field_corrections.check_notes_guard_consistent: CONFIRMED absent: inc/class-admin.php lines 281-292 — the wp_ajax_backwpup_debug_info closure has no check_ajax_referer() or current_user_can() call. The gate scored guard_consistent=false (no guard detected) which is correct — the finding is that the guard is MISSING, and source confirms it.

findings.reason: Source-verified at inc/class-admin.php:281-292. The closure registered on wp_ajax_backwpup_debug_info performs no capability or nonce check before echoing BackWPup_Page_Settings::get_information() output. Any subscriber-level authenticated user can POST to admin-ajax.php?action=backwpup_debug_info and receive debug information including absolute paths, PHP user identity, loaded extensions, temp/log folder locations, and WP-Cron URL. Output is esc_html()-wrapped (not an XSS sink), but sensitive environment data is returned without authorization. No higher-level WordPress framework guard wraps this hook — wp_ajax_* requires the callback itself to perform authorization. CONFIRMED as low-severity authenticated information disclosure.
counter_evidence: Output is escaped with esc_html() — no XSS path exists through this endpoint.
The endpoint requires WordPress authentication (wp_ajax_ prefix, not wp_ajax_nopriv_), so unauthenticated access is blocked by WordPress core.
Severity is low: data returned is server paths, PHP info, cron URL — useful for reconnaissance but not directly exploitable for RCE or data exfiltration.
dynamic_test_plan: POST /wp-admin/admin-ajax.php with action=backwpup_debug_info as a subscriber-role user (no BackWPup role). Confirm the response contains path/environment data.
Repeat the same request as an unauthenticated user. Confirm HTTP 400 or empty response (WordPress blocks nopriv actions that have no nopriv handler).
Confirm the information returned matches the output of BackWPup_Page_Settings::get_information() — specifically look for ABSPATH, document root, temp folder, log folder, PHP_SAPI user.

findings.reason: Source-verified. The admin_post_backwpup handler at inc/class-admin.php:848-895 checks only current_user_can('backwpup') before dispatching. suggested_field_corrections.check_notes_code_evidence: Sink confirmed: parts/sidebar/storage-FTP.php line 178 outputs BackWPup_Encryption::decrypt(BackWPup_Option::get($job_id,'ftppass')) in an HTML value attribute. EXTR_SKIP in BackWPupHelpers::children() does not prevent job_id injection — $job_id is not a local variable in scope before extract(), so block_data={'job_id':N} successfully sets $job_id. Path traversal guard uses realpath()+boundary check (lines 71-116) — does not restrict which named partials under parts/ are valid.

findings.reason: Full attack path confirmed from source. (1) POST to /wp-admin/rest-api/backwpup/v1/getblock with block_type=children, block_name=sidebar/storage-FTP, block_data={job_id:N} using backwpup_check authentication. (2) BackWPupHelpers::children() (inc/Utils/BackWPupHelpers.php:71-116) builds path as plugindir/parts/sidebar/storage-FTP.php, passes realpath()+boundary check (no traversal needed — the target partial is directly under parts/). (3) extract($args, EXTR_SKIP) sets $job_id=N because $job_id is not pre-set in local scope — EXTR_SKIP only protects already-defined variables. (4) parts/sidebar/storage-FTP.php line 178 decrypts the stored FTP password via BackWPup_Encryption::decrypt() and places it in an HTML value attribute. (5) The REST response returns the rendered HTML containing the decrypted plaintext FTP credential. (6) Similar paths exist for other storage provider partials (S3, Azure, etc.) exposing their respective credentials. The backwpup_check role is intended to be a low-privilege monitoring role without edit rights — it should not have access to decrypted credentials. This is a privilege escalation for credential access.
counter_evidence: Realpath()+boundary check prevents path traversal to files outside the plugin's parts/ directory. An attacker cannot escape to wp-config.php or other sensitive files.
Only partials that use extract($args) or explicitly reference $job_id will expose job-specific credentials. Partials that do not reference job options will render without credentials.
The HTML output is esc_attr()-wrapped in the value attribute — no XSS path. The credential is disclosed in plaintext within the HTML response body only.
If the job has no FTP credentials configured, the decrypted value will be empty — the impact is limited to jobs that have credentials stored.
Access requires a valid WordPress authentication cookie and the backwpup capability — unauthenticated users cannot reach this endpoint.
dynamic_test_plan: Create a BackWPup job with FTP credentials. Confirm the ftppass is stored encrypted in the database.

Verify the response HTML contains the decrypted FTP password in a value= attribute.
Repeat for block_name='sidebar/storage-S3' and other storage provider partials to confirm the scope of credential exposure.

Confirm that a user with backwpup_jobs_edit (backwpup_admin role) sees the same credentials via the normal edit-job UI — proving this is a privilege bypass, not the intended access path for backwpup_check.

suggested_field_corrections.check_notes_path_reachable: CONFIRMED: /startbackup route registered at src/Backups/API/Rest.php:96 with has_permission() = current_user_can('backwpup'). Sink: get_jobrun_url('runnow', $jobid) at line 260. Confirmed in source. backwpup_check role explicitly has backwpup_jobs_start=false (inc/class-install.php:142-158).

findings.reason: Source-verified. The /startbackup REST route uses has_permission() checking only current_user_can('backwpup'). The sink at line 260 calls get_jobrun_url('runnow', $jobid) which triggers an immediate job run. The backwpup_check role is defined at inc/class-install.php:142-158 with backwpup_jobs_start=false — this capability is intentionally denied to the check role. A backwpup_check user bypasses this intended restriction by calling the REST API directly. The backwpup_helper role (lines 162-175) has backwpup_jobs_start=true, confirming the intent is that job-starting requires at least helper privileges. The REST API does not enforce this tier.
counter_evidence: Starting a backup is generally not harmful from a data-exfiltration perspective if the backup destination is controlled by the admin.
If the backup destination has been modified by the same attacker (see storages-bac, cloudsaveandtest-bac), starting a backup could complete a two-step exfiltration chain.
Requires authenticated BackWPup access.
Resource exhaustion (running many backups) is a possible DoS vector.

suggested_field_corrections.check_notes_code_evidence: Gate flagged 'sink function backwpup_destinations::file_delete not found near line 420'. Confirmed: src/Backups/API/Rest.php line 420 contains $dest_class->file_delete($jobdest, $file) — polymorphic instance dispatch, not a static call. Gate searched for a direct symbol match but the code uses a runtime-typed variable $dest_class. Sink IS at line 420 as claimed.
suggested_field_corrections.check_notes_guard_consistent: Partial defense exists: inc/Utils/BackWPupHelpers.php lines 197-215 conditionally adds dataset-delete URLs to backup listings only when current_user_can('backwpup_backups_delete') is true. However, the /process_bulk_actions route itself checks only has_permission() = current_user_can('backwpup'). A backwpup_check user who constructs the delete request directly (without using the listing) can still call the route.

findings.reason: Source-verified. The /process_bulk_actions REST route at src/Backups/API/Rest.php:124 uses has_permission() = current_user_can('backwpup'). The route processes backup file deletion via $dest_class->file_delete($jobdest, $file) at line 420. The backwpup_check role has backwpup_backups_delete=false (inc/class-install.php:142-158). A partial defense exists: the backup listing API (inc/Utils/BackWPupHelpers.php:197-215) only includes dataset-delete URLs in API responses for users who already have backwpup_backups_delete. This means the backwpup_check UI does not show delete controls. However, the route itself has no capability check — an attacker who knows the URL structure (jobdest-top=<jobid>_<desttype> and backupfiles[]=<filename>) can call the delete route directly. The URL structure follows a predictable pattern based on job IDs and destination types that are partially observable via other read endpoints.
counter_evidence: The backup listing API does not return dataset-delete URLs to backwpup_check users, making the delete URL less discoverable through normal UI flows.
An attacker would need to know or enumerate valid backup filenames and job destination identifiers — these are not directly exposed by the listing endpoint to backwpup_check users.
Backup deletion is destructive but does not exfiltrate data.
Requires authenticated BackWPup access.
